articles.body: Project status — October 22, 2026: This is a design proposal for Cognee issue #6222 . Maintainer assignment is pending. The connector has not been implemented or tested, and there is no PR yet. This article explains the proposed scope and validation plan. Project wikis hold more than documentation. They capture why a team chose an approach, which service owns a responsibility, and what happened during an incident. A useful memory integration should preserve those notes and their source links, while also forgetting content that the author deletes. For Mergetober, the proposed contribution is a read-only connector between TiddlyWiki and Cognee.

articles.body: The standard advice for headless-browser screenshots is "default to JPEG, not PNG — it's 5-10x smaller." We wrote that rule into our own build notes while costing out a screenshot Actor, on the strength of two measurements. Then we measured it properly on a text-heavy page and it mostly evaporated — 15%, not 5-10x. So we measured it again on a photo-heavy page, to find out whether 15% was the real number or just a bad page to test on.

articles.title: Scraping E-commerce Product Data: Variants, Prices and Stock Without Losing Accuracy
articles.excerpt: E-commerce data scraping is the collection of public product information from online stores (titles, identifiers, variants, prices, availability and pack sizes) into structured records you can compare…
articles.body: E-commerce data scraping is the collection of public product information from online stores (titles, identifiers, variants, prices, availability and pack sizes) into structured records you can compare across sites and over time. Fetching the pages is rarely the hard part. Accuracy is lost in the modelling: a price attached to the wrong variant, a sale price read as the list price, or "Only 2 left" stored as free text. These are the five fields that break most often: Variant price: the page shows one price, but each size or colour has its own. Sale versus list price: two numbers on the page, and the parser picks the wrong one. Currency and number format: 1.299,00 and 1,299.00 are the same amount. Stock status: a dozen phrasings for four or five real states.

articles.title: Why Green Tests Are Not Enough for AI Coding Agents#
articles.excerpt: Over the last few months, I’ve been spending more time working with AI coding agents. They are fast, useful, and in many cases they can fix small bugs or implement focused changes much faster than doi…
articles.body: Over the last few months, I’ve been spending more time working with AI coding agents. They are fast, useful, and in many cases they can fix small bugs or implement focused changes much faster than doing everything manually. But while using them, I kept coming back to the same problem: how do I know that the evidence around the fix is actually meaningful? It is easy to ask an agent to change some code, run a test, and return a green result. The problem is that a green test only tells me that the final version passed. It does not necessarily tell me whether the test was capable of detecting the original bug. That difference sounds small, but it matters a lot. Imagine an AI agent fixes a bug and adds a regression test. The final test run passes, so the change looks good.

articles.title: # Your AI Agent Failed in Production. Can You Replay the Exact Run?
articles.excerpt: Why agent debugging needs more than prompt logs and successful final outputs. Let's say you've built an AI agent that handles customer support requests. It retrieves customer records, checks policies,…
articles.body: Why agent debugging needs more than prompt logs and successful final outputs. Let's say you've built an AI agent that handles customer support requests. It retrieves customer records, checks policies, calls external APIs, and recommends the next action. Everything works during testing. Then one day, the agent produces an incorrect recommendation. You open your logs. All you see is: Agent started Tool executed Agent completed Not particularly helpful. The real question is: Can you reconstruct the entire execution and identify exactly where things went wrong? Why debugging AI agents is different A conventional workflow generally follows a predefined path. An agent may choose its next action dynamically.

articles.title: How to Know When Your Vibe-Coded App Breaks Before Your Users Do: A 7-Step Beginner Guide to Error Alerts
articles.excerpt: Your app is live. You tested signup, you tested the main feature, everything worked. Then a week later someone replies to your launch post: "Is your site broken? I can't log in." Too often, that is ho…
articles.body: Your app is live. You tested signup, you tested the main feature, everything worked. Then a week later someone replies to your launch post: "Is your site broken? I can't log in." Too often, that is how founders find out their app is broken: from a user, days late, after other people quietly gave up and left. AI tools like Lovable, Bolt, v0, Cursor and Claude Code are great at building the happy path. They usually do not set up the part that tells you when something fails in production. This guide fixes that in an afternoon. By the end you will have three things: an error tracker that catches crashes and silent failures, an outside uptime check that notices when the app or database is down, and alerts that actually reach you. All of it starts on free plans.

A login does not protect you, and there are no official updates for PHP 8.1 and older. In industrial sites, PHP sits in the web interfaces of controllers, industrial routers and firewalls, as well as EV chargers and energy equipment whose firmware is rarely updated. Operators should cut these web interfaces off from the internet now. Vulnerable PHP web interfaces will in all likelihood still be found in industrial sites well beyond 2030. On Monday, October 26, we will host a virtual NASA Science Town Hall, from NASA Headquarters, to explain our new Competition Model 2.0 (CM 2.0), and answer your questions. We have heard you. We have listened. We know that the burden of bringing great ideas forward has been too heavy for too long. It has taken years to move mission concepts through the current two-step process. articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year.

articles.title: Bose acquires Skullcandy to help it reach a wider audience
articles.excerpt: Bose announced today it has acquired Skullcandy. Although the two companies are competitors in the consumer audio space, Skullcandy recently partnered with its new owner to bring several of Bose's aud…
articles.body: Bose announced today it has acquired Skullcandy. Although the two companies are competitors in the consumer audio space, Skullcandy recently partnered with its new owner to bring several of Bose's audio technologies - including its head-tracking spatial audio and excellent active noise cancellation (ANC) - to products like the Skullcandy Crusher 1080 ANC headphones and Method 360 ANC earbuds . Specific details about the deal weren't shared, but according to a news release, Bose plans to keep Skullcandy a separate brand that will become part of its premium consumer audio business.
